name: Anise
description: A delicate, lacy-umbelled annual of the carrot family whose small grey-green seeds taste of sweet licorice. Egyptians and Romans prized it, and Roman feasts ended with mustaceum, an anise-spiced cake eaten to settle overfull bellies. Pliny wrote that it kept the face young and the sleep free of bad dreams, and anise seeds were once paid as tithes and taxes in medieval England.
metaphysicalUses: Anise is a sweet guardian. Old herbals advise stuffing a pillow with the seeds to keep away nightmares, and a sprig of the green herb hung on the bedpost was said to restore lost youth. A wash of anise seed tea was used to consecrate tools and to cleanse the ritual space, and the seeds are added to purification baths together with bay leaves. Burned or carried, anise is believed to sharpen psychic sight and invite helpful spirits, and its fresh leaves were set about the magic circle to ward off evil. Its sweetness makes it a natural addition to happiness and sweetening workings.
medicalUses: Traditionally one of the classic carminative seeds, chewed after meals or taken as a mild tea for gas, bloating and colic, and given to nursing mothers in folk practice. It has long been added to cough syrups and lozenges to loosen phlegm and soothe a tickling throat, and the warm tea was sipped for colds and mild nausea.
whereToFind: Native to the eastern Mediterranean and southwest Asia, growing in warm, sunny, well-drained ground. It is an easy annual to sow directly in spring once frost has passed; harvest the seed heads when they turn grey-brown in late summer and dry them in paper bags. Whole aniseed is sold in grocery spice aisles, Middle Eastern and Indian markets, and herb apothecaries. Do not confuse it with star anise, an unrelated tree spice.
uses: Stuff a small dream pillow with aniseed to keep nightmares away
Brew a strong seed tea and use it, cooled, to wash and consecrate ritual tools
Add aniseed and bay leaves to a purification bath before ritual
Chew a pinch of seeds after a meal to sweeten breath and settle digestion
Scatter seeds around the circle's edge for protection during spirit work
Add to sweetening jars and happiness sachets for its sweet nature
Burn a few seeds on charcoal to open psychic awareness before divination
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Anise has mild estrogen-like activity, so avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy and with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis or fibroids. Never ingest the essential oil, which can cause nausea, vomiting and seizures, and dilute it well (about 1 to 2 percent) for skin use; keep it away from young children and cats. People allergic to the carrot family (celery, fennel, dill) may react. Wild lookalikes include deadly poison hemlock, so only use purchased or garden-grown anise. If burning on charcoal, do so only in a well-ventilated room, never in a closed space, as charcoal gives off carbon monoxide.
bestTime: Late summer, Lughnasadh to Mabon (Aug–Sep) for seed harvest
interactions: Medicinal amounts may interfere with hormonal birth control, estrogen therapy and tamoxifen because of anise's estrogen-like activity.
pets: Keep the essential oil away from cats and dogs; diffusing it around pets, especially cats, can be harmful.

name: Ashwagandha
partsUsed: roots (leaves and berries traditionally, not for home use)
description: A humble, grey-leaved shrub of the nightshade family whose small orange-red berries sit inside papery husks like tiny lanterns. Its Sanskrit name means 'smell of the horse,' for the earthy scent of its root and the stallion-like strength it was said to give. For some three thousand years it has been one of the great rasayana, or rejuvenating, herbs of Ayurveda.
metaphysicalUses: Ashwagandha is a root of steady, enduring power, worked by modern witches for strength, stamina and resilience rather than quick bursts of energy. Carry a piece of the root or a pouch of the powder in charms for courage and endurance during long trials, and place it on the altar in spells for recovery, vitality and long life. Its grounding, earthy nature makes it useful in workings to steady the nerves and root a scattered spirit, and its horse-strength lore lends it to spells for virility and passion. It pairs well with ginseng in charms of personal power.
medicalUses: In Ayurveda the powdered root is traditionally taken in warm milk with honey or ghee as a restorative tonic for exhaustion, weakness and convalescence, and to calm the nerves and promote restful sleep. It is regarded as an adaptogen, helping the body cope with stress, and has been used for nervous debility, low vitality and to support the immune system.
whereToFind: Native to India, the Middle East and parts of Africa, growing wild in dry, stony, sunny ground and waste places. It can be grown as an annual in warm gardens or large pots from seed sown in late spring; roots are dug in autumn once the berries ripen. Dried root and powder are widely sold by Ayurvedic shops, health food stores and herb suppliers; choose reputable, tested sources.
uses: Carry a piece of the dried root in a red pouch for courage and endurance
Place root powder on the altar in spells for recovery and long life
Add a pinch to grounding sachets to steady a scattered spirit
Sip a traditional warm moon milk with the powder before bedtime meditation
Bury a small piece of root in a pot of earth while stating your strength goals
Include it in lust and vitality charms for its stallion-strength lore
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (it may cause miscarriage) and while breastfeeding. It may raise thyroid hormone levels, so avoid with hyperthyroidism and use caution with thyroid medication; it may also stimulate the immune system, so use caution with autoimmune conditions. It may lower blood sugar and blood pressure and cause drowsiness. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported from supplements; stop if you notice dark urine, yellowing skin or abdominal pain. As a nightshade, avoid if sensitive to that family; do not eat the berries or leaves, and stop two weeks before surgery.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Oct) for root harvest
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives, benzodiazepines and alcohol, diabetes medication and blood pressure medication, and may interfere with thyroid hormone and immunosuppressants.

name: Bee Balm
description: A shaggy-headed member of the mint family whose ragged crimson or lavender blooms draw bees, butterflies and hummingbirds all summer long. Its scent recalls the bergamot orange, which gave it one of its names. Indigenous peoples of eastern North America used it as medicine for generations, and after the Boston Tea Party colonists drank Oswego tea, learned from the Oswego people, in place of English tea.
metaphysicalUses: Bee balm is a bright, joyful herb of success and sweet attraction. Its fragrant leaves are added to sachets and charm bags to clarify the mind, lift a heavy mood and draw prosperity and good fortune, much as the flowers draw bees to the garden. Burn the dried leaf or add it to a bath to release melancholy and invite restful sleep. Because pollinators and hummingbirds flock to it, it is grown in faery and pollinator gardens as an offering to the small spirits of the land, and its red blooms add warmth to love and friendship workings.
medicalUses: Traditionally the leaves and flowers were brewed into a warming tea for colds, sore throats, fevers and coughs, and as a carminative for gas, bloating and nausea. Rich in thymol, like thyme, it was used as an antiseptic wash and poultice for skin infections and minor wounds, and steam from the tea was inhaled for congestion.
whereToFind: Native to eastern and central North America, growing along stream banks, woodland edges, meadows and moist clearings. It grows easily in gardens in sun or part shade and spreads readily; harvest leaves and flowers in midsummer while in full bloom and dry them on screens. Plants are sold at garden centers and native plant nurseries, and dried herb is available from some herb suppliers.
uses: Brew a cheerful tea of leaves and petals to lift a heavy mood
Add dried leaves to money and success sachets to draw prosperity
Grow it in a pollinator garden as an offering to the faery folk
Toss a handful into a ritual bath to release melancholy before sleep
Use the scarlet petals in love and friendship jars for warmth
Make a strong cooled infusion as an antiseptic wash for minor scrapes
caution: Generally safe in tea amounts for adults. Avoid it in pregnancy, including strong teas, because it has traditionally been used to bring on menstruation and may raise the risk of miscarriage, and avoid it while breastfeeding because safety is unknown. Its thymol content may irritate sensitive skin or stomachs. Use caution if allergic to the mint family.
bestTime: Midsummer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug) while in full bloom

name: Blessed Thistle
description: A sprawling, bristly annual with spiny leaves and small yellow flowers cradled in prickly bracts. Its name honors St. Benedict, and medieval monks grew it in cloister gardens as a cure-all, even against the plague. In 'Much Ado About Nothing,' Margaret prescribes Carduus Benedictus as the only thing for a qualm at the heart.
metaphysicalUses: Blessed thistle is a protective and purifying herb of Mars, used to break hexes and send ill-wishing back where it came from. Carry it or add it to a bath for strength and vitality, especially when feeling drained or under spiritual attack, and burn it to cleanse a space of curses. It was worn as an amulet against evil and against the plague, and as a holy herb it is used to bless people, objects and homes. Its spines make it a natural guardian at windows and thresholds, and it is said to be sacred to Pan, bringing wild, life-giving energy to spells.
medicalUses: Traditionally a bitter tonic taken in small amounts before meals to stimulate appetite and digestion, ease gas and support a sluggish liver. In folk practice it was given to nursing mothers to encourage milk flow, and hot infusions were taken to bring on a sweat and break fevers.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean region and southern Europe, growing on dry, stony waste ground and field edges, and naturalized in parts of the Americas. It can be grown from seed sown in spring in full sun; harvest leaves and flowering tops just as it begins to flower in summer, wearing gloves. Dried herb is sold by herb suppliers and apothecaries.
uses: Hang a dried bundle at the window as a spiny guardian against ill will
Add to an uncrossing bath to strip away hexes and restore vitality
Burn the dried herb with salt to cleanse a room after a curse
Carry a sprig in a red pouch for strength when feeling spiritually drained
Use in house blessings as a holy herb of St. Benedict
Place in a mirror box or reversal jar to send ill-wishing back
caution: Avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding in medicinal amounts. Large doses (over about 5 grams a day) can cause stomach irritation, vomiting and diarrhea. Avoid with stomach ulcers, acid reflux or inflammatory bowel conditions, as it increases stomach acid. People allergic to ragweed, daisies, artichokes and other Asteraceae plants may react.
bestTime: High summer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug) at first flowering
interactions: It increases stomach acid and may reduce the effect of antacids, H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors; use caution with blood-thinning medication.

name: Boneset
description: A tall, hairy wetland plant crowned with flat clusters of fuzzy white flowers, its stem seeming to pierce straight through each joined pair of leaves. Early settlers thought this joined leaf signaled the power to knit bones, and leaves were once wrapped with bandages around splints. Its true fame came from breakbone fever, a flu so painful it felt as though the bones were breaking.
metaphysicalUses: Boneset is a Saturnine herb of protection and exorcism. An infusion sprinkled around a home or room drives off evil spirits, and it is used in protective sachets to guard health, especially in seasons of sickness. Its joined leaves make it a herb of mending, worked in sympathetic spells to knit together what is broken and to heal fractures in body, family or friendship. It also has a place in banishing workings meant to break a long, stubborn illness or misfortune.
medicalUses: One of the most widely used remedies of 19th-century North America, boneset was learned from Indigenous healers and taken as a hot, bitter infusion at the onset of flu and fevers to induce sweating, ease aching bones and muscles, and break the fever. Cold infusions were taken as a bitter tonic. It was a household staple in settler homes, often hung in attics to dry.
whereToFind: Native to eastern North America, growing in wet meadows, marshes, ditches, swamp edges and along streams. It flowers from midsummer to early autumn; cut the flowering tops when the blossoms first open and dry them thoroughly before any use. It can be grown in a moist, sunny garden or rain garden. Dried herb is sold by some herb suppliers.
uses: Sprinkle a cooled infusion around the home to drive out unwanted spirits
Add dried boneset to a health-protection sachet during cold and flu season
Use its joined leaves in a mending spell to heal a broken friendship
Hang a dried bundle in the attic as old settlers did, for household health
Place on the altar in banishing work against a lingering illness or misfortune
Grow it in a rain garden for pollinators and as a living ward
caution: Use only the dried herb; the fresh plant can cause nausea and vomiting. Large doses are strongly emetic and laxative and can cause severe diarrhea. Boneset contains unsaturated pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can damage the liver with repeated use, so use only briefly if at all, and avoid entirely with liver disease, in pregnancy, while breastfeeding and for children. People allergic to ragweed and the daisy family may react. Consult a healthcare provider before use.
bestTime: Late summer, Lughnasadh to Mabon (Aug–Sep) at first bloom
interactions: No well-documented interactions; avoid combining with other liver-stressing herbs or medications.

name: Chickweed
partsUsed: aerial parts (leaves, stems, flowers), fresh or dried
description: A tender, sprawling little plant of cool damp ground whose tiny white flowers, each with five deeply split petals, look like scattered stars. It is one of the first greens of the year and keeps growing through mild winters, and its name comes from the poultry who love it. Old country folk watched it as a weather sign: when the flowers stay closed, rain is coming.
metaphysicalUses: Chickweed is a soft, lunar herb of love and fidelity. Carry it or add it to sachets to attract love or to keep a relationship faithful and true, and use it in spells to draw tender, nurturing affection. Its star-shaped flowers and watery nature make it a lovely addition to moon rituals and moon water, and its humble, healing nature suits spells for emotional healing and self-love. Gathered from the garden edge, it is a gentle reminder that magic grows underfoot.
medicalUses: Traditionally a cooling, soothing herb, made into salves, poultices and infused oils for itchy, inflamed skin, eczema, rashes, minor burns, insect bites and splinters. The fresh greens were eaten as a spring tonic in salads and soups, and the tea was taken as a mild diuretic and to soothe irritated digestion.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and now found almost worldwide in gardens, lawns, field edges, damp waste ground and shady paths. It is most lush in cool weather in early spring and autumn; snip the top few inches of the leafy stems with scissors. Check for a single line of hairs along the stem to identify it. Dried herb and chickweed salves are sold by herb suppliers.
uses: Carry a sachet of dried chickweed to keep a relationship faithful
Steep fresh sprigs in spring water under a full moon to make a moon water
Make a cooling chickweed salve for itchy skin and bug bites
Add a handful of fresh greens to a spring salad as a seasonal tonic
Tuck it into self-love and emotional healing pouches
Lay the star-flowered stems on the altar during moon rituals
caution: Generally safe as a food and external remedy, though some people are allergic to it on the skin. Large amounts may cause digestive upset, and medicinal amounts in pregnancy or while breastfeeding have not been shown to be safe, so stick to food amounts. Avoid harvesting from fertilized lawns or roadsides, as it can accumulate nitrates and pollutants. Learn to distinguish it from lookalikes such as scarlet pimpernel and spurges, which are toxic; spurges have milky sap.
bestTime: Early spring, Imbolc to Ostara (Feb–Apr), and again in cool autumn
pets: Chickweed contains nitrates and has caused nitrate poisoning in grazing livestock that ate large amounts.

name: Cleavers
description: A scrambling, clinging plant whose stems and leaves are covered in tiny hooked hairs that stick to clothing, fur and anything that brushes past. Its whorls of narrow leaves look like little green stars along the stem. Country folk once used bundles of it as sieves for straining milk, and its close relative Lady's Bedstraw stuffed the mattresses of old.
metaphysicalUses: Cleavers is a herb of tenacity and holding fast. It is used in spells to bind, to bind together, and to strengthen relationships, commitments and agreements so that they hold. Woven into a wreath or cord, it makes a protective binding for the home, and its clinging stems make it a fitting ingredient in friendship and reconciliation charms. Fresh cleavers juice or tea is also used in spring cleansing rituals to carry away winter's stagnation.
medicalUses: Traditionally a spring tonic and gentle cleanser, the fresh plant was steeped in cold water or juiced to support the lymphatic system, ease swollen glands and act as a mild diuretic for the kidneys and urinary tract. It was applied as a poultice or wash to skin conditions, minor wounds and inflamed areas.
whereToFind: Native across Europe, Asia and North Africa, and widespread in North America, growing in hedgerows, woodland edges, gardens and damp waste ground. It is best gathered in spring before it sets its hooked seeds; it is most potent fresh, losing much of its virtue when dried. Dried herb is sold by some herb suppliers.
uses: Braid fresh stems into a cord to bind and strengthen a commitment
Hang a wreath of cleavers over the door as a protective binding
Steep fresh sprigs in cold water overnight for a spring cleansing drink
Add to friendship and reconciliation charms so the bond clings fast
Lay fresh strands across a petition paper to hold your intention
Use as a fresh poultice on minor skin irritations
caution: Generally considered safe in usual amounts. It is traditionally used as a diuretic, so check with a healthcare provider if you have kidney disease or take diuretics or lithium. The juice may affect blood sugar; people with diabetes should monitor closely. The hooked hairs can cause contact irritation in sensitive people. Avoid it in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, since its safety has not been established.
bestTime: Spring, Ostara to Beltane (Mar–May) while young and green
interactions: May add to the effects of diuretic medication; monitor blood sugar if taking diabetes medicines.

name: Galangal
latin: Alpinia officinarum (lesser galangal), Alpinia galanga (greater galangal)
description: A tall, ginger-like plant of Southeast Asia whose knobbly, reddish rhizome tastes of pepper, pine and citrus. It came west along the spice routes and was a favorite medicine of Hildegard of Bingen, who called it the 'spice of life.' In Hoodoo it is known as Little John to Chew, the little brother of High John the Conqueror, and is famous for its use in court cases.
metaphysicalUses: Galangal is a fiery root of luck, protection and victory in legal matters. In Hoodoo the root is chewed, then the juice spat on the floor of the courtroom before the judge enters, or carried in a mojo bag, to win a court case. It is carried for protection, luck, health and lust, and added to money spells and sachets to draw prosperity. Powdered and burned, it breaks hexes and curses, and it brings power and drive to any working in which you need to prevail.
medicalUses: Traditionally a warming digestive root, taken as a tea or chewed to ease nausea, indigestion, gas, colic and seasickness, much like ginger. It has long been used in Asian and European folk medicine to warm the body, stimulate circulation and help shake off colds and chills.
whereToFind: Native to southern China, Indonesia and Southeast Asia, growing in warm, humid, partly shaded forest ground. It can be grown in pots indoors or in tropical gardens from a fresh rhizome; roots are dug after about a year. Fresh greater galangal is sold in Asian groceries, and dried lesser galangal root is sold by Hoodoo suppliers, apothecaries and spice merchants.
uses: Carry a piece of root in a mojo bag to court for a favorable outcome
Grind and add to money powder or sachets to draw prosperity
Burn powdered root on charcoal to break hexes and curses
Carry with High John root for power and personal victory
Add fresh slices to soups and curries for warming digestion
Sprinkle powdered root across the threshold for protection
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It may cause heartburn or stomach upset in large amounts. If burning on charcoal, do so only in a well-ventilated room, never in a closed space, as charcoal gives off carbon monoxide.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Oct) for root harvest; work any time before a court date
interactions: Medicinal amounts may interact with blood-thinning medication and antacids or acid-reducing drugs.

name: Holy Basil
partsUsed: leaves, flowering tops, seeds, stems (for prayer beads)
description: A bushy, purple-tinged basil with a spicy, clove-like scent, revered in India as the earthly form of the goddess Tulsi, consort of Vishnu. Nearly every traditional Hindu home keeps a tulsi plant in a raised shrine in the courtyard, watered and circled in prayer each morning and evening. Its woody stems are carved into mala beads worn by devotees of Krishna.
metaphysicalUses: Holy basil is a herb of devotion and divine protection. A living tulsi plant guards the home and keeps it pure, and its presence is said to open a household to blessings and prosperity. Its leaves are offered on altars, added to holy water, and carried for protection, and malas of its wood are used in prayer and mantra meditation to deepen spiritual practice. It is worked in fidelity and love spells, reflecting Tulsi's devotion, and its purifying smoke and fragrance clear negativity before ritual. Approach it with the reverence it holds in living Hindu tradition.
medicalUses: In Ayurveda, tulsi is a revered adaptogen taken daily as a tea to help the body meet stress, calm the mind and support the immune system. It is a traditional remedy for colds, coughs, sore throats, fevers and bronchial congestion, often brewed with ginger and honey, and is also used for indigestion and as a general tonic for long life.
whereToFind: Native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, growing in warm, sunny places. It grows well in pots in full sun and can be overwintered indoors as a perennial in cold climates; pinch leaves regularly and harvest just as it begins to flower. Plants are sold at herb nurseries, and dried tulsi tea is widely available at health food stores, Indian groceries and apothecaries.
uses: Keep a living tulsi plant near the front door to protect and bless the home
Sip a tulsi tea before meditation to calm the mind and open the heart
Offer fresh leaves on the altar with a lit lamp in morning devotion
Add leaves to holy water or a blessing wash for purification
Use a tulsi-bead mala for mantra and prayer practice
Carry a few dried leaves in a fidelity charm for devoted love
Brew with ginger and honey for a soothing cold-season drink
caution: Generally safe as a tea. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy, while breastfeeding and when trying to conceive, as animal studies suggest it may affect fertility. It may lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting, so use caution with diabetes or bleeding disorders and stop two weeks before surgery.
bestTime: Summer, Litha to Mabon (Jun–Sep), harvested just before flowering
interactions: May add to the effects of blood-thinning and diabetes medications; possible interaction with sedatives.

name: Honeysuckle
latin: Lonicera periclymenum (also L. caprifolium, L. japonica)
partsUsed: flowers, leaves, stems (berries are not used)
description: A twining, climbing vine whose creamy, trumpet-shaped flowers pour out their sweetest perfume at dusk to call in the moths. Its habit of wrapping tightly around trees made it a symbol of devoted love and clinging affection, and Shakespeare's Titania sleeps in a bower of woodbine. Children have long pinched the flowers to sip the single drop of nectar inside.
metaphysicalUses: Honeysuckle is a sweet, binding vine of prosperity and devoted love. Green candles ringed with the flowers draw money, and honeysuckle is added to money and luck sachets to attract abundance. Lightly crushing the fresh flowers and rubbing them on the forehead is said to heighten psychic powers, and its dusk-blooming nature suits it to evening divination. Grown around the house, it brings good luck and protection, and its twining stems are woven into love charms to bind two hearts together in faithful affection. In Scottish lore a honeysuckle walking stick was a lucky charm.
medicalUses: In Chinese medicine the flower buds of Japanese honeysuckle (jin yin hua) are a classic cooling remedy for sore throats, colds, fevers and hot, inflamed skin conditions. European folk healers made a syrup of the flowers for coughs and sore throats, and used the leaves as a cooling wash for skin and mouth sores.
whereToFind: European honeysuckle grows wild in hedgerows, woodland edges and thickets across Europe; Japanese honeysuckle is widespread and invasive in eastern North America. Harvest flowers in early summer on a dry morning, choosing only blossoms, and grow native or non-invasive species on a trellis or fence. Dried flowers are sold by herb suppliers and Chinese herb shops.
uses: Ring a green candle with honeysuckle blossoms in a money spell
Rub a fresh flower lightly on the forehead before divination
Grow it around the front door for luck and protection
Weave the twining stems into a love knot for faithful affection
Add dried flowers to prosperity sachets and wallet charms
Make a simple flower syrup to soothe a sore throat
caution: The flowers are safe in modest amounts, but the berries of most honeysuckle species are mildly to moderately toxic and should never be eaten, especially by children and pets. Make sure plants are correctly identified. Japanese honeysuckle may slow blood clotting, so avoid medicinal amounts with bleeding disorders and stop two weeks before surgery. Japanese honeysuckle is invasive in many regions; check before planting.
bestTime: Early summer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jul) while in fragrant bloom
interactions: Medicinal amounts of Japanese honeysuckle may add to the effects of anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs such as warfarin.
pets: Keep berries away from dogs and cats; they can cause vomiting and diarrhea.

name: Horsetail
description: A living fossil from the age of the dinosaurs, when its ancestors grew as tall as trees. Its jointed, hollow, ridged stems carry whorls of thin green branches like a horse's tail and are so rich in silica that they were used to scour pots, polish pewter and sand wood. Children pull the segments apart and fit them back together like a puzzle.
metaphysicalUses: Horsetail is an ancient herb of endurance and the deep past. It is used in fertility charms, and its jointed stems are said to charm snakes, giving it a place in serpent and transformation magic. As a plant that has survived for hundreds of millions of years, it lends strength and longevity to spells and connects the practitioner with the oldest ancestors of the green world. Its scouring nature makes it a fitting broom herb for scrubbing away stubborn energy, and its whistle, made by blowing through a hollow stem, was used to call spirits.
medicalUses: Traditionally a mineral-rich herb taken as a short course of tea to strengthen hair, nails and bones, and as a diuretic for the urinary tract and mild fluid retention. It was applied as a poultice or wash to stop bleeding and help wounds heal, and used as a gargle for mouth sores.
whereToFind: Native across the Northern Hemisphere, growing in damp ground, ditches, stream banks, railway embankments and moist waste places. Gather the green, branched summer stems, not the brown spring fertile shoots, and dry them. Be certain of the species: marsh horsetail (Equisetum palustre) is toxic. It spreads aggressively, so grow it only in a contained pot. Dried herb is sold by herb suppliers.
uses: Tie stems into a small broom to scour stubborn energy from corners
Place a sealed jar of dried stems on the ancestor altar to honor the deep past
Carry a jointed stem in a fertility charm
Use a hollow stem as a whistle in rites to call spirits
Rinse hair with a cooled infusion for strength and shine
Lay stems across a candle plate in spells for endurance
caution: Use only for short periods. Horsetail contains thiaminase, which destroys vitamin B1, so avoid long-term use and avoid with alcohol use disorder or thiamine deficiency. As a diuretic it can deplete potassium; avoid with kidney disease, heart disease, gout or diabetes. Not for children, pregnancy or breastfeeding. Contains small amounts of nicotine. Correctly identify it, as marsh horsetail is poisonous to people and livestock.
bestTime: Early to midsummer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jul) for green stems
interactions: May interact with diuretics, lithium (raising its levels), digoxin and other heart medication through potassium loss, and diabetes medication.
pets: Toxic to livestock, especially horses, in quantity.

name: Lilac
description: A beloved spring shrub whose heavy cones of purple, mauve or white blossoms fill the air with unforgettable perfume for a few short weeks. Greek myth tells that the nymph Syrinx, fleeing Pan, was turned into a reed, and Pan made his pipes from it; lilac's Latin name honors her. In New England, lilacs planted by settlers often still bloom beside the vanished cellar holes of old farmhouses.
metaphysicalUses: Lilac is a gentle but effective herb of exorcism and protection. Planted around the home or placed in vases indoors, its fresh blossoms are said to drive away evil and banish lingering spirits, and in New England it was planted to keep ghosts away. It is a herb of beauty and love, added to glamour and attraction magic, and its sweet, nostalgic scent calls up memories of past lives and loved ones gone before. Lilac flowers on the altar bring a soft, peaceful energy to spirit work and remembrance.
medicalUses: In folk medicine lilac leaves and fruit were brewed as a bitter tea to bring down fevers, and the flowers and leaves were made into poultices and washes for minor skin complaints, rashes and cuts. Today it is mostly valued for its edible flowers, which are candied or infused into syrups.
whereToFind: Native to the rocky hills of the Balkans, it is widely planted in gardens and naturalized near old homesteads across Europe and North America. Cut flower sprays in mid to late spring as they open, early in the day, and dry them quickly or use fresh. Shrubs are sold at every garden center. True lilac essential oil is rare; most lilac fragrance is synthetic.
uses: Place vases of fresh lilac around the house to drive away unwanted spirits
Plant lilac near the property line as a protective boundary
Add dried petals to beauty and glamour baths
Set lilacs on the ancestor altar during spring remembrance
Infuse the flowers in honey or sugar for a sweetening spell
Hold a blossom during meditation to recall past lives and old memories
caution: True lilac (Syringa) is not listed as toxic, and the flowers are edible in small amounts (they can taste bitter or green). Eat only flowers you are sure are Syringa and that are free of pesticides; never eat florist, garden-center or roadside flowers. Try a small amount first, since some people react to the pollen or strong scent. Do not confuse it with Persian lilac (chinaberry, Melia azedarach), a different tree that is poisonous. Bark and leaves are best not eaten.
bestTime: Spring, Ostara to Beltane (Apr–May) during the brief bloom
pets: True lilac is low in toxicity to animals, but keep pets and horses from chewing the bushes or clippings. Persian lilac (chinaberry) is poisonous to dogs, cats and horses.

name: Linden
latin: Tilia cordata (also Tilia platyphyllos, Tilia × europaea)
partsUsed: flowers with bracts, leaves, inner bark
description: A tall, graceful tree with heart-shaped leaves whose hanging clusters of creamy flowers fill early summer evenings with a honeyed scent and the hum of bees. In Ovid's tale, the devoted old couple Philemon and Baucis were turned into an oak and a linden standing side by side. Across Germany and the Slavic lands the village linden was the center of community life, where dances were held and justice was given.
metaphysicalUses: Linden is a tree of love, peace and protection. Its branches hung over the door guard the home, and the flowers are used in love spells and in sleep pillows for calm, restful nights. Germanic peoples held court beneath the linden, believing it brought out the truth, so it is a fine tree for justice and legal matters. It is associated with immortality and long life and with the goddesses of love and the hearth, and its heart-shaped leaves are carried as charms of lasting, faithful love. Carrying the bark is said to prevent intoxication.
medicalUses: Linden flower tea is one of the great European folk remedies, sipped to calm nervous tension, ease anxiety and bring restful sleep, especially for children. Taken hot, it induces gentle sweating to help break fevers and colds, and it has long been used to relax and support the heart and circulation and to ease tension headaches.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia, with American basswood (Tilia americana) in eastern North America, it grows in mixed woodlands and is widely planted along streets and in parks. Gather the flowers with their pale bracts in early summer, when freshly opened, and dry them in the shade. Dried linden flowers are sold by herb suppliers, tea shops and European groceries.
uses: Fill a sleep pillow with dried linden flowers for peaceful rest
Hang a linden branch over the door for protection
Sip linden blossom tea before a calming meditation
Carry a heart-shaped leaf as a charm of faithful love
Sit beneath a linden tree to seek truth before a legal decision
Add the flowers to a love bath with rose petals
caution: Generally safe as a tea. Use only freshly dried flowers, as old ones may cause nausea. Frequent heavy use is not advised for people with heart conditions. Rare allergic reactions occur.
bestTime: Early summer, around Litha (Jun–Jul) when the flowers open
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives and blood pressure medication, and its mild diuretic effect may raise lithium levels.

name: Magnolia
description: An ancient flowering tree, older than the bees, whose large waxy blossoms evolved to be pollinated by beetles. The glossy-leaved Southern magnolia, with its huge, lemony-scented white flowers, is the emblem of the American South. In China, magnolia bark and buds have been used in medicine for over two thousand years.
metaphysicalUses: Magnolia is a herb of fidelity and lasting love. Place a leaf or a few dried petals under the bed, or keep them in the bedroom, to keep a partner faithful. It is used in love and beauty spells and in Southern conjure to bless a home and keep it peaceful. As one of the oldest flowering trees, magnolia is also linked to longevity, endurance and wisdom, and the fragrance of its blossom calms and soothes in rituals of peace.
medicalUses: In traditional Chinese medicine the bark of Magnolia officinalis (hou po) is used to ease anxiety, stress and tension, and to settle digestion, bloating and coughs, while the flower buds (xin yi) are used for nasal congestion, sinus trouble and allergies. In the American South the bark of native magnolias was used in folk practice for fevers.
whereToFind: Southern magnolia is native to the southeastern United States, growing in rich, moist lowland forests, and is widely planted as an ornamental in warm climates. Gather fallen leaves and blossoms in late spring and summer; petals bruise easily and dry best on a flat screen. Trees are sold at nurseries, and magnolia bark and buds are sold by Chinese herb shops and supplement suppliers.
uses: Place a magnolia leaf under the mattress to keep a partner faithful
Add dried petals to love and beauty sachets
Write a wish on a fallen leaf and keep it on the altar until it comes true
Float a fresh blossom in a bowl of water for a peaceful home
Include magnolia in a house blessing for calm and endurance
Burn dried leaves in rites of longevity and steady wisdom
caution: Magnolia bark is sedating; avoid it in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and do not combine with sedatives, alcohol or sleep medication. It may slow blood clotting, so stop two weeks before surgery. Bark products have been linked to kidney damage reports, likely through contamination or mix-ups with toxic Aristolochia herbs, so use bark and bud supplements only from reputable sources and under the guidance of a qualified practitioner. Some people are allergic to the pollen.
bestTime: Late spring to midsummer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jul) in bloom
interactions: May increase drowsiness with sedatives, sleep medications, barbiturates and alcohol, and may raise bleeding risk with blood thinners and aspirin.

name: Mexican Marigold
description: A sturdy, strongly scented annual with great pompom heads of brilliant orange and gold. The Aztecs called it cempoalxóchitl, 'twenty flower,' and it is the flower of the dead at Día de Muertos, when its petals are scattered in paths from the street to the ofrenda so the spirits can find their way home by its color and scent. It is not the same plant as pot marigold (Calendula).
metaphysicalUses: Mexican marigold is the great herb of ancestor reverence. Garlands and arches of cempasúchil frame ofrendas, and petal paths guide beloved dead back to the family table during Día de Muertos; it is also used to honor the dead at Samhain and on ancestor altars at any time. Its blazing solar color carries warmth, joy and protection, chasing away gloom and banishing harmful spirits. Grown around the home, it protects and brings cheer, and its petals are used to soothe grief and to remember those who have passed with love.
medicalUses: In Mexican folk medicine an infusion of the flowers and leaves was taken for indigestion, colic, gas and stomach pains, and used as a wash for skin complaints, sore eyes and minor wounds. The flowers are rich in the yellow pigment lutein and have been used as a natural dye and food coloring.
whereToFind: Native to Mexico and Central America, growing in sunny, open, dry places. It is easy to grow from seed in full sun as a summer annual and blooms until frost; cut flowers in autumn at their peak and dry the heads whole or as loose petals. Plants and cut flowers are sold widely in autumn, especially near Día de Muertos at Mexican markets and garden centers.
uses: Scatter a path of petals from the door to the ancestor altar to guide the dead home
Drape a garland of cempasúchil over a photograph of a loved one who has passed
Plant them around the garden and doorstep for protection and cheer
Place a bowl of fresh blooms on the altar for sun magic and joy
Hold the flowers while speaking aloud memories of the dead to ease grief
Add dried petals to Samhain incense blends
caution: Can cause contact dermatitis and allergic reactions in people sensitive to the daisy family. Avoid internal medicinal use in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Do not confuse with pot marigold (Calendula) when making remedies. Keep Tagetes essential oil off skin that will be exposed to sun, as it can be phototoxic.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain and Día de Muertos (Sep–Nov 2)
pets: May cause mild stomach upset and skin irritation in dogs and cats if chewed.

name: Milk Thistle
description: A tall, statuesque thistle with glossy leaves marbled in white veins and fierce purple flower heads. Christian legend says the white markings were left by drops of the Virgin Mary's milk as she nursed the infant Jesus beneath its leaves. Its seeds have been used for the liver for at least two thousand years, from Pliny to the present day.
metaphysicalUses: Milk thistle, like all thistles, is a herb of protection, strength and defiance, its spines guarding against negativity and ill will. Grown in the garden or hung by the door, it protects the home, and it is carried for courage and vitality in difficult times. Its legend of Mary's milk makes it a herb of nurturing protection and purification, used in healing workings to cleanse and restore, and in spells to strengthen one's resilience. Thistles were sacred to Thor and were thought to protect against lightning.
medicalUses: The seeds have been used for centuries as a traditional liver tonic, taken to support and protect the liver and gallbladder, and to aid digestion and the flow of bile. The young leaves and stems were once eaten as a spring vegetable after the spines were removed. Today seed extracts standardized for silymarin are among the most widely used herbal supplements.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean and southern Europe, it grows in sunny, dry waste places, field edges and roadsides, and is naturalized and considered an invasive weed in parts of the Americas and Australia. Harvest seed heads in late summer when the fluff appears, wearing thick gloves. Seeds, powders and capsules are sold by health food stores and herb suppliers.
uses: Grow a milk thistle by the garden gate as a spiny guardian
Carry seeds in a red pouch for courage and vitality in hard times
Place a dried flower head on the altar in healing and purification spells
Hang a dried thistle by the door to guard the home against ill will
Add seeds to a protective sachet for nurturing, motherly protection
Sprinkle seeds around a candle in spells for resilience
caution: Milk thistle is not a substitute for medical treatment: liver disease, jaundice or suspected mushroom poisoning are emergencies that require a doctor, not home remedies. It may cause digestive upset, loose stools, headache or allergic reactions, especially in those allergic to ragweed and the daisy family. It may lower blood sugar and may have estrogen-like effects, so avoid with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis or fibroids. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding without advice.
bestTime: Late summer, Lughnasadh to Mabon (Aug–Sep) for seed harvest
interactions: May lower blood sugar with diabetes medication, and may change levels of drugs processed by the liver, including warfarin, diazepam, raloxifene, sirolimus and some hepatitis C drugs.

name: Orris Root
latin: Iris germanica var. florentina (also Iris pallida)
partsUsed: dried, aged rhizome (root), external use only
description: The dried rhizome of the white Florentine iris, which slowly develops a sweet, violet-like fragrance only after being aged for two to three years. It has been a perfume fixative since ancient Egypt and Greece, and Florence still bears the iris on its coat of arms. Queen Elizabeth I is said to have worn its powder, and the iris flower is named for the Greek goddess of the rainbow.
metaphysicalUses: Orris root is one of the great love-drawing herbs. The powder, known as Love Drawing Powder, is dusted on the body, clothes, sheets and letters to attract love, and a whole root is carried in a mojo bag to draw a lover or keep a partner close. In Hoodoo a whole root called a 'Queen Elizabeth Root,' sometimes said to resemble a woman's figure, is used for power and control in relationships. Orris is hung in the home for protection, and a root on a string was used as a pendulum for divination. As a fixative it is added to incense, oils and sachets to bind their scents and their power together.
medicalUses: Historically, orris root was chewed to sweeten the breath and used in tooth powders, and herbalists once gave small amounts for coughs and congestion. These internal uses are no longer considered safe because fresh iris root is toxic and the dried root is a well-known allergen. Today it is used only externally as a fragrance fixative.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean and long cultivated around Florence, Tuscany and Morocco, it grows in sunny, well-drained, chalky soil. Rhizomes are dug after two or three years and must be dried and aged for years before their scent develops. Dried orris root, whole and powdered, is sold by Hoodoo suppliers, perfume and soap suppliers, and apothecaries.
uses: Dust a little orris powder on your sheets or letters to draw love (patch test first)
Carry a whole root in a red mojo bag to attract a lover
Use a Queen Elizabeth root in spells for power in a relationship
Hang a root on a string and use it as a pendulum for divination
Add a pinch of powder to incense, sachets and potpourri as a fixative
Hang a piece of root in the home for protection
caution: Not for internal use. Fresh iris root is toxic and can cause severe vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain, and the dried root can also upset the stomach. Orris powder is a well-documented allergen that can trigger sneezing, asthma, hay fever and skin rashes; avoid inhaling the fine powder and patch test before any skin contact. Keep away from children and pets, and avoid during pregnancy.
bestTime: Summer to autumn, Lughnasadh to Mabon (Aug–Sep) for digging rhizomes
pets: Iris rhizomes are toxic to dogs and cats, causing drooling, vomiting and diarrhea; keep roots and powder out of reach.

name: Poppy
latin: Papaver somniferum (also Papaver rhoeas, corn poppy)
partsUsed: seeds (culinary), dried flowers and seed heads (decorative and symbolic only)
description: Silky, short-lived flowers of scarlet, white or lilac that drop their petals within a day to reveal a crowned seed capsule. In Greek myth Demeter gathered poppies to ease her grief for Persephone, and Hypnos and Morpheus were shown crowned with them, scattering sleep. Since the First World War, the red corn poppy blooming over the battlefields of Flanders has been the emblem of remembrance for the fallen.
metaphysicalUses: Poppy is the flower of sleep, dreams and the borderland between life and death. The seeds are added to love and fertility charms, carried for luck and to draw money, and scattered in spells for abundance, as each pod holds countless seeds. Old lore says that carrying a dried pod, or soaking seeds in wine, can grant invisibility. Dried seed heads are kept on the altar for dream work, remembrance and to honor the dead, and red poppies are offered to ancestors and fallen warriors. Work with poppy symbolically; its magic lies in the seed, the flower and the image, not in its drugs.
medicalUses: Historically, the latex of the opium poppy was the source of opium, morphine and codeine, among the most important and most dangerous medicines in human history, and corn poppy petals were made into syrups for coughs and restlessness in children. These uses are now understood to be dangerous and are not for home practice; only the seeds are used as food today.
whereToFind: The opium poppy is native to the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia; the corn poppy grows wild in fields, roadsides and disturbed ground across Europe. Ornamental poppies grow easily from seed scattered in early spring or autumn, and dried seed heads can be gathered in late summer for decoration. Culinary poppy seeds are sold in grocery stores; growing or possessing opium poppies for anything other than ornament or seed is illegal in many places, so check local laws.
uses: Add culinary poppy seeds to love and fertility charm bags
Keep a dried seed head on the bedside altar for dream work
Scatter poppy seeds in a prosperity spell for countless blessings
Lay red poppies on the ancestor altar for remembrance of the fallen
Carry a dried pod in a pouch as an old charm of invisibility
Bake poppy seeds into ritual bread for a Lughnasadh or Mabon feast
caution: DANGER: only culinary poppy seeds are safe to eat. The latex, pods, unwashed seeds, straw and 'poppy tea' contain opiates that can cause addiction, respiratory failure and death, and fatal overdoses from homemade poppy seed tea have occurred; never brew or ingest any part of the plant other than store-bought seeds used in normal food amounts. Corn poppy is also mildly toxic to people and livestock. Eating poppy seed foods can trigger a positive opiate drug test. Keep pods and flowers away from children and pets. Cultivation laws vary by country.
bestTime: Summer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug); Remembrance Day (Nov 11) for honoring the dead
interactions: Any opiate-containing poppy product is dangerous with alcohol, benzodiazepines, sleep aids and other sedatives or opioids.
pets: Poppy plants and pods are toxic to dogs and cats and can cause sedation or agitation.

name: Self-Heal
description: A low, creeping member of the mint family with stubby purple flower spikes that dot lawns and meadows all summer. Its old names, carpenter's herb and sicklewort, recall the cuts and gashes of laborers it was used to heal, and its flowers were thought to resemble a hook or a throat, showing by the doctrine of signatures that it healed both. Today it is found on nearly every continent.
metaphysicalUses: As its name says, self-heal is a herb of healing in body, mind and spirit. Carry it or place it on the altar in healing spells for yourself and others, and add it to baths and sachets for emotional healing and self-love, especially after heartbreak or burnout. It is said to protect against harm and help you recover your own strength, and its humble, earthy nature makes it a grounding and balancing herb for those who give too much of themselves. Medieval folk believed it could drive away the Devil.
medicalUses: Traditionally a wound herb, crushed fresh leaves were applied to cuts and bruises to stop bleeding and speed healing, and the tea was used as a gargle for sore throats, mouth ulcers and inflamed gums. In Chinese medicine the flower spikes (xia ku cao) are a cooling herb for swollen glands, headaches and red, sore eyes.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, Asia and North America, it grows in lawns, meadows, woodland clearings, field edges and along paths. It flowers from early summer to autumn; gather the flowering tops in full bloom and dry them. It is easy to grow as a ground cover in sun or part shade. Dried herb is sold by herb suppliers and Chinese herb shops.
uses: Place a sprig on the altar in a healing spell for a loved one
Add it to a self-love bath after heartbreak or burnout
Carry a sachet of dried self-heal to support recovery and resilience
Gargle a cooled tea for a sore throat or mouth sore
Grow it as a lawn ground cover and leave it for the bees
Apply a fresh leaf poultice to a minor cut or bruise
caution: Generally considered safe. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It may lower blood sugar, so use care with diabetes medication. Allergic reactions are rare.
bestTime: Summer, Litha to Mabon (Jun–Sep) in full flower
interactions: May add to the blood-sugar-lowering effect of diabetes medication.

name: Sunflower
partsUsed: seeds, petals, flower heads, stalks, seed oil
description: A towering North American annual whose great golden heads follow the sun across the sky while young. Indigenous peoples of the Americas domesticated it thousands of years ago, and it was sacred in Inca sun worship. In Greek myth the nymph Clytie, pining for the sun god Helios, was turned into a flower that forever turns to follow him.
metaphysicalUses: Sunflower carries the joy and power of the sun. Cut a sunflower at sunset while making a wish, and it is said that the wish will be granted before another sunset passes, provided it is not too greedy. Eating the seeds is believed to aid fertility, and sleeping with a sunflower under the bed was thought to reveal truth in dreams. It is a herb of wisdom, honesty, health and happiness, and its seeds are used in abundance and success spells, as each head holds hundreds of them. Sunflowers on a Lughnasadh or Litha altar honor the sun at its height.
medicalUses: Folk healers used a tea of the petals and seeds for coughs, colds and chest complaints, and infusions of the leaves were used to bring down fevers. Sunflower seed oil, mild and rich in vitamin E, has long been a soothing base for massage and for dry, irritated skin, and the nutritious seeds have been a staple food.
whereToFind: Native to North America, growing in open prairies, dry plains and disturbed ground. It is one of the easiest annuals to grow from seed in full sun; sow in late spring and harvest seed heads in late summer or autumn when the backs turn yellow-brown. Seeds, oil and plants are sold at grocery stores, garden centers and farm stands.
uses: Cut a sunflower at sunset while making a wish
Place sunflowers on the Litha or Lughnasadh altar to honor the sun
Eat a handful of seeds as part of a fertility working
Add petals to a happiness bath or sun water
String dried seeds into a garland for abundance
Use sunflower oil as a carrier for success and sun magic oils
Leave a seed head in the garden as an offering for birds and land spirits
caution: Generally safe. People allergic to ragweed, daisies, chrysanthemums, marigolds and other Asteraceae may react to the pollen, petals or oil. Seed shells can cause digestive blockage if eaten in large amounts. A diet high in sunflower oil may raise blood sugar in people with diabetes.
bestTime: Late summer, Litha to Lughnasadh and Mabon (Jul–Sep) at peak bloom
interactions: Large dietary amounts of sunflower oil may interfere with diabetes medicines.
pets: Sunflowers are non-toxic to pets, but avoid salted seeds and shells.

name: Tobacco
partsUsed: dried leaves (offering and symbolic use only)
description: A tall, sticky-leaved plant of the nightshade family with trumpet-shaped flowers of white, pink or green, native to the Americas. For thousands of years it has been one of the most sacred plants of many Indigenous nations, offered in prayer and ceremony to carry words to the Creator and the spirits. In Afro-Caribbean and Hoodoo traditions it is a classic offering to spirits, and in the Andes and Amazon mapacho is a plant of powerful healers.
metaphysicalUses: Tobacco is above all an offering plant. A pinch of loose tobacco left at the foot of a tree, at a crossroads, or on running water carries thanks and prayers to the spirits of the land, and it is offered before gathering herbs in the wild as a gift in return. In Afro-diasporic traditions it is a favored offering for Papa Legba, Elegguá, Ogun and the ancestors. Sealed in a jar or pouch, tobacco is used as an offering vessel and to protect a home from harmful spirits. Many Indigenous nations hold tobacco as sacred; if you work with it, do so humbly and avoid imitating closed ceremonies.
medicalUses: Historically, tobacco was used in many cultures as a poultice for stings, bites and wounds, as a smoke for toothache, and even as an enema in 18th-century Europe. It is now known to be highly toxic and addictive, and none of these uses are safe today.
whereToFind: Native to tropical and subtropical South and Central America, now grown across the world as a commercial crop, and ornamental Nicotiana species are grown in gardens. Loose leaf tobacco is sold in tobacco shops, and ceremonial and offering tobacco is sold by some Indigenous-run businesses and spiritual suppliers. Garden tobacco grows easily from seed in full sun; wear gloves when handling wet leaves.
uses: Leave a pinch of loose tobacco at a tree's roots as thanks before foraging
Offer tobacco at a crossroads in road opening work
Place a small dish of tobacco on the ancestor altar as an offering
Seal tobacco in a jar with protective herbs to guard the home
Grow ornamental Nicotiana in a moon garden for its evening-scented flowers
Wrap a pinch in red cloth as a prayer offering to the spirits of the land
caution: POISONOUS: all parts of the tobacco plant contain nicotine, a potent toxin. Never eat, brew or make remedies from it. A single swallowed cigarette or a small amount of loose tobacco can seriously poison a child or pet, and nicotine liquids can be fatal. Handling wet green leaves can cause 'green tobacco sickness' through the skin, so wear gloves. Smoking and chewing tobacco are addictive and cause cancer and heart and lung disease. Keep all tobacco, including outdoor offerings, well out of reach of children and animals.
bestTime: Late summer, Lughnasadh to Mabon (Aug–Sep) for leaf harvest; offerings any time
pets: Highly toxic to dogs and cats; eating tobacco or nicotine products causes vomiting, tremors, seizures and can be fatal. Call a vet or pet poison line right away.

name: Turmeric
partsUsed: rhizomes (roots), fresh or dried and powdered
description: A leafy relative of ginger whose knobbly rhizome, when cut, glows a startling golden orange. It has been used in India for some four thousand years as a spice, a dye and a sacred substance, staining the robes of monks and the foreheads of worshippers. In the Hindu haldi ceremony before a wedding, a paste of turmeric is spread on the bride and groom to bless, purify and protect them.
metaphysicalUses: Turmeric is a golden herb of purification and protection. Sprinkle it around a space, mix it with salt, or add it to a wash to cleanse and seal a home, a ritual area or tools. In Hindu tradition it is used in blessings, on thresholds and in wedding rites to purify and draw good fortune, and it is sacred to Ganesha and to goddesses of abundance. Its blazing color makes it a natural for sun magic, success and prosperity, and its healing reputation lends it to health spells. A pinch of turmeric in a candle working or charm bag adds radiant, protective energy.
medicalUses: In Ayurveda and folk medicine across Asia, turmeric is a beloved anti-inflammatory, taken in food or warm golden milk for aching joints, sluggish digestion and liver support. A paste of turmeric was applied to cuts, scrapes and blemishes as an antiseptic and to soothe and brighten the skin, and turmeric with honey was a home remedy for coughs and colds.
whereToFind: Native to South and Southeast Asia, growing in warm, humid, partly shaded tropical ground. It can be grown in large pots from a fresh rhizome in warm conditions, harvested when the leaves die back after eight to ten months. Fresh rhizomes are sold in Asian groceries and some supermarkets, and the powder is in every spice aisle; choose tested brands, as cheap powders have been found adulterated with lead.
uses: Mix turmeric with salt and sprinkle across the threshold to protect the home
Add a pinch to a floor wash to purify and bless a space
Dress a gold or orange candle with turmeric in success and sun spells
Sip golden milk with turmeric, black pepper and honey as a healing ritual
Draw a protective symbol in turmeric paste on a doorstep for blessings
Carry a dried rhizome in a charm bag for prosperity and health
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. High-dose supplements can cause stomach upset and, rarely, liver injury, especially in products combined with black pepper extract (piperine). Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy, with gallstones or bile duct problems, bleeding disorders, and stop two weeks before surgery. It may reduce iron absorption. It stains skin, fabric and surfaces.
bestTime: Late autumn to winter, Samhain to Yule (Nov–Dec) when the leaves die back for harvest
interactions: Supplements may increase bleeding risk with warfarin and other blood thinners, add to diabetes medication, and interact with acid-reducing drugs.

name: Witch Hazel
partsUsed: bark, twigs, leaves (distilled water and extracts, external use)
description: A small, spreading tree of eastern North American woods that blooms in late autumn and winter, with spidery yellow ribbon-like petals glowing on bare branches. Its seed pods ripen a year later and burst open with a snap, flinging seeds several yards. Its name comes from the Old English 'wice,' meaning pliant, and its forked branches have long been used as divining rods to find water and buried treasure.
metaphysicalUses: Witch hazel is a herb of protection, healing and finding what is hidden. A forked branch of witch hazel is the traditional divining rod, used to dowse for water, lost objects and buried treasure, and wands of its wood are used for protection and divination. It is said to mend a broken heart and cool passions, so it is used in spells for emotional healing and release after a loss. Its winter blooming makes it a herb of hope in dark times, and distilled witch hazel is a handy base for spiritual sprays and cleansing washes.
medicalUses: Indigenous peoples of North America taught settlers to use witch hazel bark and leaves as a soothing wash for bruises, sprains, swellings and insect bites. Distilled witch hazel water is still a popular household astringent, applied externally to minor cuts, scrapes, bruises, skin inflammation, varicose veins and hemorrhoids, and as a gentle facial toner for oily skin.
whereToFind: Native to the woodlands of eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida, growing at forest edges, in understories and along streams. It is an excellent garden shrub for winter interest; cut twigs and bark in autumn or late winter. Distilled witch hazel is sold in every pharmacy, and dried bark and leaf are sold by herb suppliers.
uses: Cut a forked branch to use as a divining rod for water or lost things
Use distilled witch hazel as the base for a spiritual cleansing spray
Dab distilled witch hazel on bug bites and minor bruises
Carry a twig in a pouch to soothe a broken heart
Make a witch hazel wand for protection and divination
Plant a witch hazel near the house for winter hope and protection
caution: Distilled witch hazel is for external use only, and many commercial products contain alcohol; never drink it. The bark and leaves are rich in tannins and taken internally can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting and constipation, and large amounts may harm the liver. Avoid internal use, especially in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It may dry or irritate sensitive skin; patch test first and keep away from the eyes. Alcohol-based sprays are flammable, so keep them away from candles.
bestTime: Late autumn to winter, Samhain to Imbolc (Oct–Feb) when it blooms

name: Yew
partsUsed: wood, branches, needles (symbolic and craft use only; never ingested)
description: A dark, slow-growing evergreen with flat, glossy needles and soft red berry-like cups, among the longest-lived trees in Europe; some churchyard yews are believed to be over two thousand years old. Its branches root where they touch the ground, and old trunks hollow and regrow, making it an emblem of death and rebirth. Yew longbows won medieval battles, and some scholars think Yggdrasil, the Norse world tree, was a yew rather than an ash.
metaphysicalUses: Yew is the tree of death, rebirth and the eternal. It stands guard in churchyards and ancient sacred sites, and is linked to the dead, to ancestor work and to communion with spirits. The ogham letter Idho is the yew, meaning endings, transformation and the cycle that turns death into new life. Wands and staves of yew wood are prized for necromancy, spirit work and deep protection, and rune sets and ogham staves are carved from it for divination. Meditating near an ancient yew opens a path to ancestral memory, but do so with respect and never lie for long beneath it, as old lore warned.
medicalUses: The yew has no safe folk medicinal use, and historical attempts to use it led to many deaths. In modern medicine, compounds derived from the Pacific and European yew are processed in laboratories into the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel (Taxol), which shows the plant's power but not a home remedy.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, growing in chalk and limestone woods, upland ravines and especially churchyards; related yews grow in North America and Asia. It is widely planted as hedging and topiary. Gather fallen twigs or wood with gloves, and buy finished yew wands and staves from reputable woodworkers rather than cutting ancient trees.
uses: Carry a finished yew wand in necromancy and ancestor work
Carve or buy a set of yew ogham staves for divination
Meditate beside an ancient churchyard yew on ancestral memory
Place a sprig in a sealed glass jar on the Samhain altar to honor the dead
Draw the ogham Idho in your grimoire as a symbol of rebirth
Plant a yew hedge as a living boundary of protection, away from grazing animals and children's play areas
caution: POISONOUS: every part of the yew except the fleshy red aril is deadly, including the needles, bark, wood, sawdust and the seed inside the aril. It contains taxine alkaloids that can stop the heart, sometimes within hours and with few warning signs, and there is no reliable antidote. Never eat, brew, burn as incense, or make remedies from any part of it. Wear gloves and a dust mask when working the wood, and wash hands afterward. Keep yew clippings away from children, pets and livestock; a small amount can kill a horse.
bestTime: Samhain to Yule (Oct–Dec), the dark half of the year
pets: Deadly to dogs, cats, horses and livestock; even small amounts of needles or clippings can cause sudden death.

name: Yerba Santa
description: An aromatic evergreen shrub of the California hills, with long, sticky, resin-coated leaves and clusters of pale lavender trumpet flowers. Chumash, Miwok and other Indigenous Californian peoples have long used it as medicine, and Spanish missionaries named it 'holy herb' after learning of its healing power. It is one of the first plants to return after wildfire.
metaphysicalUses: Yerba santa is a herb of healing, protection and emotional release. It is carried for beauty, health and psychic powers, and worn around the neck or added to healing spells and sachets. Many modern practitioners use it to support grief and heartbreak, believing it helps release emotions held in the chest, and its fragrant smoke is used to purify and protect a space. As a plant that rises after fire, it is also a herb of renewal and resilience. It is a gentle, locally abundant alternative to over-harvested white sage, but honor the Indigenous traditions it comes from.
medicalUses: Traditionally a premier respiratory herb, yerba santa tea or chewed leaves were used to loosen phlegm and ease coughs, colds, congestion, sore throats and asthma, and the leaves were smoked by Indigenous Californians for chest complaints. A poultice of the leaves was applied to sores, bruises and aching joints.
whereToFind: Native to California and southern Oregon, growing on dry, rocky slopes, chaparral and open hillsides. It can be grown in dry, sunny, well-drained native gardens. Harvest leaves sparingly in spring and summer, with permission and gratitude, and dry them flat. Dried leaves and bundles are sold by herb suppliers and Native-owned businesses.
uses: Burn a dried leaf to purify a space as a sustainable alternative to white sage
Carry a sachet of yerba santa over the heart while grieving
Add the leaves to healing and protection charm bags
Sip a tea of the leaves with honey for a cough or cold
Hold a leaf before divination to open psychic awareness
Grow it in a native garden as a symbol of renewal after hardship
caution: Generally safe in tea amounts. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. The tannins may reduce iron absorption, and it may interfere with medication taken at the same time. Smoke can irritate the lungs, especially with asthma, so burn it only with good ventilation. Some people may have allergic or skin reactions to the resin.
bestTime: Spring to summer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jun) while in flower
interactions: Its tannins may reduce absorption of iron and oral medications taken at the same time; separate doses by a few hours.
